findings.sink: Shell command execution in downstream functions (generateRootCertificate, generateSignedCertificate, installAuthority) that pass commonName to openssl via child_process
findings.missing_control: The regex was changed from a strict allowlist [a-zA-Z0-9.] to (.|\.) which matches any character except newlines, permitting shell metacharacters such as ;, |, &, $(), and backticks

The new regex accepts it, and when the value is interpolated into an openssl shell command (e.g. openssl req -subj "/CN=${commonName}"), the semicolon terminates the openssl invocation and the attacker's command executes with the process's privileges.

The new regex (.|\.) is equivalent to .+ (any non-newline character, 1–64 long), so shell metacharacters now pass validation and reach openssl command strings, enabling arbitrary command execution.

The params file in the temp directory is created with default permissions (often 0644). Another local user reads the file while the child process is running and obtains the serialized environment variables, command, and options. The removed stdout/stderr lockdown can also allow local users to read sensitive command output.

findings.title: Removal of dunder-key guard allows attacker-controlled attribute injection on dataclass instances

The code calls getattr(instance, '__class__') to obtain the class object, recursively processes the nested dict against that class, and then calls setattr(instance, '__class__', result). This can change the instance's runtime type (if a size-compatible class is reachable) or corrupt `__dict__`, altering application state, bypassing type-based authorization checks, or triggering unexpected code paths in downstream logic that relies on the dataclass's type or attribute layout.

The finding's claims of type confusion and authorization bypass are not supported by the code path.

An attacker supplies `tol=0.05); DROP TABLE users; --` as the query parameter. The value is interpolated directly into the Oracle SQL string, resulting in: `ST_AREA(geom, 0.05); DROP TABLE users; --)` — executing arbitrary SQL.

return self.as_sql(

    template="%%(function)s(%%(expressions)s, %(tolerance)s)",

    **extra_context

findings.title: Request keyword denylist can be bypassed by placing a benign object before the prohibited field
findings.source: Attacker-controlled update/object body passed to DatabaseController.update/create and checked by Utils.checkProhibitedKeywords
findings.sink: Utils.objectContainsKeyValue returns early on the first object/array value, so later top-level fields are not scanned
findings.missing_control: Complete recursive traversal of all top-level fields; the function should continue the loop after recursing instead of returning the recursion result
findings.exploit_scenario: With requestKeywordDenylist configured to block key 'malicious' value 'payload', an attacker sends update {benign: {}, malicious: 'payload'}. objectContainsKeyValue recurses into benign, finds no match, returns false, and never checks malicious, so the request is accepted.
findings.explanation: The newly added denylist check is fail-open when a prohibited keyword appears after the first nested object/array, defeating the configured security control.
findings.fix_snippet: if (['[object Object]', '[object Array]'].includes(Object.prototype.toString.call(v))) { if (Utils.objectContainsKeyValue(v, key, value)) return true; }

findings.title: Open redirect via unsanitized request.fullpath in get_bad_url_redirect_path
findings.source: HTTP request path in request.fullpath
findings.sink: Returned path used as an HTTP redirect Location/URL by the caller
findings.missing_control: No validation that the derived path is a safe same-origin relative URL; leading '//' and other URL authority characters are preserved
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker requests a path such as //evil.com/pkg on the pypiserver host. The function returns //evil.com/simple/pkg/, which browsers and pip treat as a protocol-relative URL and redirect to evil.com.
findings.explanation: The parent path is taken directly from the request, so an attacker can control the authority part of the generated redirect, enabling open redirect/phishing or redirecting package clients to an attacker-controlled host.

llm_json.source: HTTP request path via request.fullpath — an attacker controls it by requesting a URL like http://pypiserver.example.com//evil.com/pkg, causing the client to send GET //evil.com/pkg HTTP/1.1
llm_json.sink: The returned string is used as the HTTP 302 Location header by the caller, producing a protocol-relative URL //evil.com/simple/pkg/ that browsers resolve to http(s)://evil.com
llm_json.control: None. The function takes request.fullpath verbatim, strips a trailing slash, takes the parent via rsplit, and appends /simple/{prefix}/. No check ensures the result is a same-origin relative path (no leading //, no scheme, no authority).
llm_json.counterevidence: The caller code is not shown in the diff, so the exact redirect mechanism (302 vs 301, header name) is inferred from the function name and docstring. In practice, pip and most package clients do not follow browser-style protocol-relative redirects, limiting the attack surface to web browsers. However, the open-redirect primitive is real and the function is newly introduced by this change.
llm_json.reason: get_bad_url_redirect_path is a new function added in this diff that builds a redirect target directly from the attacker-controlled request path without sanitising leading '//' or an embedded authority. A crafted request path like //evil.com/pkg yields a protocol-relative Location header that redirects the victim's browser to an attacker-controlled host, constituting a concrete open-redirect (CWE-601) introduced by this change.
